beats.lead: IBM's 1956 RAMAC 350 gets filed away as 'the first hard drive, five whole megabytes.'
beats.text: That number depends entirely on which bits you count.
beats.note: The Computer History Museum's own figure for it is 3.75 megabytes, not 5.

beats.text: It stored 5 million characters, but each one took 8 bits on the disk — only 6 of those bits were actual data, the rest was parity and spacing.
beats.note: Count all 8 bits per character and you get the famous 5MB. Count only the informational 6, and it's 3.75MB.

beats.name: IBM 350 RAMAC
beats.role: Reynold Johnson's team at IBM's San Jose lab built it: fifty 24-inch magnetic disks spinning on a single spindle, the first commercial hard drive.

beats.text: IBM only leased the whole 305 RAMAC system — disk drive, processor, printer, card punch, all together.
beats.note: The unit weighed over a ton, moved by forklift, occasionally flown in on cargo planes.

beats.context: The monthly lease for the whole system in 1956 — about $36,700 in today's money, and the drive still wasn't yours to keep.

beats.lead: The capacity ceiling wasn't a technical one either.
beats.text: IBM's own engineers said the drive could have held more.
beats.note: Marketing turned it down — they didn't yet know how to sell anyone on wanting more storage than that.

beats.line: A ton of steel, rented by the month, for less data than gets argued about in the comments today.
